title: Semantic HTML for Accessibility
summary: The accessibility tree is what assistive tech actually reads, and it's built almost entirely from the semantic HTML you write. Learn how it differs from the DOM, and why a native element beats an ARIA-patched div every time.

slides.markdown:
Every visual browser renders the DOM into pixels. Every screen reader, switch device, and voice-control tool renders a parallel, text-based structure called the **accessibility tree** — and it's built almost entirely from the semantic meaning of your HTML, not its visual appearance.

This is the single fact that makes semantic HTML an accessibility requirement rather than a nice-to-have: a `<div>` styled to look exactly like a button is invisible to the accessibility tree as a button. It just doesn't exist there as an interactive control, no matter how convincing it looks on screen.

This topic covers what the accessibility tree actually is, how native elements populate it correctly for free, and the landmark/heading structure that lets assistive tech users navigate a page without reading it top to bottom.

slides.subTitle: How the browser exposes the DOM to assistive tech
slides.markdown:
The browser builds the accessibility tree from the DOM automatically, computing three things for every node that matters: its **role** (what kind of thing it is — button, link, heading, textbox), its **accessible name** (the label a screen reader announces — from text content, `aria-label`, or an associated `<label>`), and its **state** (checked, expanded, disabled, current value).

Purely decorative elements — a `<div>` used only for layout, an image marked `alt=""` — are typically pruned from the tree entirely, since they carry no meaning worth announcing. This is why the accessibility tree is usually smaller and flatter than the full DOM: it represents *meaning*, not markup structure.

A screen reader never touches the DOM directly — it queries the accessibility tree through the operating system's accessibility API. If a node's role, name, or state is wrong or missing in that tree, no amount of correct visual styling fixes it, because the screen reader never sees the visual layer at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Native elements come with behavior for free
slides.subTitle: <button> vs <div onclick>
slides.markdown:
A `<button>` element automatically gets: the `button` role in the accessibility tree, keyboard focusability (it's in the natural tab order without any `tabindex`), activation on both Enter and Space, and disabled-state handling (`disabled` removes it from the tab order and marks it non-interactive to assistive tech, all in one attribute).

A `<div onclick="...">` styled identically gets **none of this**. To match a real button's behavior you'd need `role="button"`, `tabindex="0"`, a `keydown` handler checking for both Enter and Space (the two keys differ in which event fires the click in some implementations — a frequent source of a "works with Enter, silently fails with Space" bug), and manual `aria-disabled` handling that still doesn't remove it from tab order the way native `disabled` does.

The same logic scales across every native element: `<a href>` gets keyboard activation and the `link` role for free; `<input type="checkbox">` gets the `checkbox` role, `Space` toggling, and `checked` state tracking for free. The rule worth internalizing: **reach for the native element first**, and only fall back to a generic element plus ARIA when no semantic option covers the interaction pattern you need.

slides.subTitle: <nav>, <main>, <header> and screen-reader navigation
slides.markdown:
Screen reader users rarely read a page top to bottom the way a sighted user scans it — most screen readers offer a shortcut to jump directly between **landmark regions**, letting a user skip straight to `<main>` without hearing the entire navigation menu and header read aloud first on every single page.

The landmark elements that matter most: `<header>` (introductory content, usually top-of-page or top-of-section), `<nav>` (a block of primarily navigational links), `<main>` (the primary content unique to this page — should appear exactly once), `<footer>` (closing content), and `<aside>` (content tangential to the main content, like a sidebar).

A page built entirely out of `<div>`s with visually identical layout gives a screen reader user zero landmark navigation — they're forced to tab or read through everything linearly, every single time, on every single page, which is a real, measurable tax on browsing speed that sighted users never pay because they can visually scan and jump straight to what they want.

slides.subTitle: Why skipping levels breaks navigation-by-heading
slides.markdown:
The second major screen-reader navigation shortcut, alongside landmarks, is jumping between headings — most screen readers let a user pull up a full list of a page's `<h1>`–`<h6>` headings and jump to any one directly, effectively using heading structure as a table of contents.

That only works if heading levels form a genuine hierarchy: one `<h1>` per page (the page's title), `<h2>`s for its major sections, `<h3>`s for subsections within an `<h2>`, and so on — never skipping a level for visual reasons (using `<h4>` instead of `<h2>` purely because the design calls for smaller text at that spot). Skipping levels doesn't break rendering, so it's an easy, invisible mistake to ship — but it does break the heading-list navigation shortcut, since a user jumping through headings sequentially hits confusing gaps that don't reflect the page's actual structure.

The fix when a design wants smaller-looking text at a given heading level: use CSS to restyle the correctly-leveled heading, never pick a heading level for its default font size.

Before: ```html
Home
About
``` This renders identically to the fixed version below but is invisible as navigation to a screen reader, unreachable by keyboard, and contributes nothing to the accessibility tree beyond plain unstyled text. After: ```html
Home About
``` The fix costs nothing in visual flexibility — every property you could apply to the `

slides.sectionTitle: A clickable div invisible to keyboard and screen reader
slides.markdown:
The most common real-world instance of this whole topic's lesson: a designer hands over a mockup with a card that's "clickable anywhere," and the fastest implementation is `<div class="card" onclick="navigate()">`. It works perfectly for a mouse user and fails completely for two other groups simultaneously — a keyboard-only user can't Tab to it at all (divs aren't focusable by default), and a screen reader user hears it announced as plain, non-interactive text with no indication anything is clickable.

The fix isn't necessarily "make the whole div a button" — that can create nested-interactive-element problems if the card contains its own links or buttons. A common correct pattern wraps just the primary click target (usually the card's title) in a real `<a href>` and uses a CSS technique (an absolutely positioned pseudo-element, or a full-card `<a>` that other interactive children escape via `position: relative; z-index`) to keep the whole card visually clickable while keeping exactly one real, accessible link as the actual interactive element.

The test that catches this reliably: unplug the mouse and try to reach every clickable thing on the page using only Tab and Enter.

slides.sectionTitle: When ARIA is the only option
slides.markdown:
Semantic HTML doesn't cover every interaction pattern a real UI needs — there's no native `<tabs>` or `<combobox>` element with built-in accessible behavior, which is exactly the gap [ARIA Roles, States, and Properties](aria-roles-states-properties) exists to fill for custom widgets that have no native equivalent.

The ordering matters, though: semantic HTML is always the first choice when a native element exists for the job, because it gives you the accessible behavior for free and correctly, with no chance of the ARIA attributes drifting out of sync with the actual UI state. ARIA is the tool for the genuine gaps — a custom dropdown, a tab interface, a live region announcing dynamic content — not a general substitute for choosing the right element in the first place.

This is the throughline the rest of this group builds on: get the semantic foundation right first, and ARIA only has to cover the parts HTML genuinely can't express.

A handful of quick checks catch most semantic gaps before they ship: open your browser devtools' Accessibility panel and inspect a few key elements — does a clickable card show up with a role at all, or nothing? Does an icon-only button have an accessible name, or does it read as "button" with no label? Pull up the page's heading outline (devtools or a browser extension) and confirm it reads as a genuine hierarchy, not a jumble of levels chosen for font size.

A fast manual pass: unplug the mouse and Tab through the whole page — everything clickable should be reachable, in a sensible order, with a visible focus indicator at every stop. This single test catches the single most common failure (`<div onclick>`) faster than any automated tool, because automated tools generally can't determine whether something *should* be interactive, only whether the markup that *is* interactive follows the rules correctly.

A strong answer to "why does semantic HTML matter for accessibility" names the mechanism, not just the conclusion: assistive technology doesn't read your DOM or your CSS directly — it queries the accessibility tree, a separate structure the browser computes from your markup's *semantic* meaning. Native elements populate that tree correctly, with the right role, name, and state, automatically. Generic elements (`<div>`, `<span>`) populate it with nothing, by design, because they carry no semantic meaning of their own.

That's why `<div onclick>` isn't a style choice with a minor accessibility downside — it's a functional gap: the accessibility tree simply has no button there for a screen reader or switch device to find, regardless of how convincingly it looks like one on screen.

The practical takeaway to close with: reach for the native element first, always; use landmarks and a correct heading hierarchy so users can navigate structurally, not just linearly; and treat ARIA as the tool for the specific gaps semantic HTML can't cover, not a general-purpose fix for having picked the wrong element.
